stubs.angle: Asks what an anemic domain model is, why entities with only getters and setters plus service classes holding all rules is a problem, and when it is still acceptable.
stubs.answerHinge: In an anemic model the behaviour and invariants live in services outside the data they protect, so any code can put an entity into an invalid state; a rich model keeps rules in entity methods, which pays off only when the domain has real rules and not for plain CRUD.

stubs.angle: Asks how organising code by vertical feature slices differs from organising it by technical layers, and what each choice does to the files touched by a typical change.
stubs.answerHinge: Layer folders spread one feature across every layer so a change touches many places and couples features through shared layer abstractions, while vertical slices keep a feature's request, logic and data access together and let each slice choose its own complexity, at the cost of possible duplication between slices.

stubs.angle: Asks which listed benefit requires microservices and cannot be obtained from a well-built modular monolith.
stubs.answerHinge: Enforced module boundaries, per-module data schemas and team ownership are all achievable inside a modular monolith, but deploying and scaling one module independently of the others needs separate deployable services.

stubs.angle: Asks the reader to select which responsibilities belong in an application service (use case handler) and which belong in the domain model.
stubs.answerHinge: An application service orchestrates a use case - loads the aggregate through a repository, calls its domain methods, commits the unit of work and maps results to DTOs - while business invariants and decisions belong in the domain entities and domain services.

stubs.angle: A BCL-only Order aggregate enforces a maximum total in AddLine, but the caller changes a line's quantity directly and the program prints a total above the limit; the reader clicks the line that lets the invariant be bypassed.
stubs.answerHinge: The public setter on OrderLine.Quantity lets code change a child entity without going through the aggregate root, so the root never re-checks its invariant; the fix is to make the line's quantity changeable only through a root method such as Order.ChangeQuantity.

stubs.subtopic: DDD strategic design and context maps
stubs.angle: Asks the reader to select the true statements about context map relationships such as conformist, anti-corruption layer, open host service, published language and shared kernel.
stubs.answerHinge: A conformist downstream adopts the upstream model as is, an anti-corruption layer translates it to protect the downstream model, an open host service with a published language offers one well-documented protocol to many consumers, and a shared kernel is a small jointly owned model that both teams must change together.

stubs.angle: Given an Order aggregate with OrderLine children and a Customer aggregate, asks which set of repositories a DDD design should define.
stubs.answerHinge: Repositories are defined only for aggregate roots (Order and Customer), because child entities such as OrderLine are loaded and saved through their root, and a repository per table would let code modify children outside the aggregate's consistency boundary.

stubs.subtopic: CQRS with a separate read store
stubs.angle: Asks how to handle a user who submits a command and then immediately sees stale data because the read model is updated asynchronously, and what the options cost.
stubs.answerHinge: With an asynchronously projected read model a read right after a write can miss it, so the design must choose deliberately: return the result or version from the command and update the UI optimistically, wait or poll until the projection reaches that version, read that one view from the write side, or tell the user the change is processing.

stubs.angle: Asks whether domain entities in a clean or DDD-style .NET application can be mapped directly by EF Core or need separate persistence models, and what EF Core features make direct mapping workable.
stubs.answerHinge: EF Core can map domain entities without attributes through Fluent API configuration in the infrastructure layer, private setters, backing fields for encapsulated collections and parameterised constructors, so a separate persistence model is usually unnecessary duplication unless the domain model and the schema really diverge.

stubs.angle: A senior engineer proposes storing the state of every service as an event stream starting with the next project, and the tech lead must decide and set the scope.
stubs.answerHinge: Event sourcing pays off only where an audit trail, temporal queries or rebuilding projections are real requirements, and it brings event schema versioning, replay and snapshot handling, eventual consistency and a learning curve, so the lead limits it to a pilot in one justified bounded context with an ADR and exit criteria rather than a system-wide mandate.
